latin.467: Ad firmandam hanc tuam rationem citas ratiocinationem Apostoli probantis Abrahamum fuisse justificatum, quia credidit Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam. Quis unquam sperasset inde posse effici, primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus hominibus imputari immediate, & quidem ad hanc poenam, corruptionem scilicet haereditariam? Nam haec est nostra quaestio, cujus affirmatio tibi formaliter concludenda fuit. Subtilem profecto te esse oportet, ac mirum artificem argumentorum, qui ex huiusmodi locis conficere illam imputationem possis.
latin.468: Sed quid inde concludis? (nam omnia tua verba huc transferre operosum esset, nec necessarium.) Quemadmodum igitur, inquis, homo justificatur & beatus est, quia credit in eum qui justificat impium; & fides eius illi imputatur ad justitiam sine operibus, quia peccatum non imputatur, sequitur ex regula contrariorum, hominem damnari & miserum esse qui non credit in Deum, quia peccatum illi imputatur ad condemnationem. Concedo. Addis, & in genere omne peccatum quod commisit. Fateor. Subjungis, & in specie hoc peccatum Adami, quod ipsum constituit peccatorem. Hoc jam nego, siquidem, ut par est, per peccatum Adami ejus peccatum actuale intelligis, necnon imputationem immediatam.
latin.469: Id enim (ut habet eruditissimus Chamierus) nos peccatores constituit non formaliter, sed causaliter; qua de re suo loco. Haec sola invenisti in vetere Testamento, quibus illam imputationem concludi posse putares. Potuissem & responsiones meas magnorum Theologorum authoritate fulcire, & iisdem ex locis alia argumenta promere tuis infesta: sed consulo brevitatem, & nolo te nimia argumentorum profusione legentem fatigare.
latin.470: Loca in quibus Deus visitare dicitur iniquitatem patrum in filios hic ne commemorata quidem: vidisti enim ea esse ad tuendam adversus mea argumenta, quam ad probandam imputationem peccati actualis Adami, magis accommodata. Revera enim inde nullum argumentum confici potest, quod non aeque de aliis Adami peccatis ac de primo, deque aliorum parentum nostrorum peccatis, ac de Adami procedat: & limitatio illa in quartam generationem repugnat aperte imputationi illimitatae in omnes generationes: & altera illa limitatio in iis qui me oderunt praesupponit odium Dei in iis qui visitantur: cum imputatio primi peccati actualis nullum in infantibus vitium praesupponat, sed, si tibi creditur, faciat. Verum de his locis alibi.
latin.471: Nunc mihi licet ita argumentari. Si dogma de imputatione primi peccati actualis Adami omnibus & singulis hominibus verum est & credendum, utique revelatum est alicubi in veteri Testamento. Atqui nullibi revelatum est in veteri Testamento. Non igitur est verum & credendum. Minor patet ex hac nostra disputatione. Majorem probo, quia lex comparata est ad detegendum & patefaciendum peccatum: per legem est cognitio peccati. Non fungitur autem suo hoc munere, uti par est, si non patefacit illud peccatum quod est omnium hominum commune, quod est omnium aliorum causa, unde omnium hominum condemnatio pendet. Non patefacit autem secundum tuam sententiam, qui peccatum ejusmodi vis esse primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus hominibus imputatum, nisi haec imputatio ex lege, seu vetere Testamento colligi possit.
latin.472: Deinde, si peccatum illud actuale omnibus imputatur proxime, idque tenentur homines credere, nititur imputatio illa lege aliqua, cuius etiam ope cognosci debet, eaque valde antiqua. Cum igitur nulla ejusmodi lex occurrat in veteri Testamento, nullam esse illam imputationem fatendum est. Denique Israelitae increduli, qui ante Christi adventum mortui sunt, judicati sunt secundum legem quam a Deo per manum Mosis acceperunt. Atqui secundum legem damnari non potuerunt immediate ob peccatum actuale Adami, nec ipsis illud imputari, nisi secundum legem constare potuerit id peccatum eorum singulorum fuisse peccatum. Idem de omnibus aliis hominibus dicendum. Fit enim omnis judiciaria imputatio peccati & inflictio poenae secundum aliquam legem. Atqui imputatio immediata peccati actualis omnibus hominibus & vitii inhaerentis inflictio, si, ut tu ais, est; utique judiciaria est. Fit igitur secundum aliquam legem. Eam ergo, si potes, profer. Nulla certe deprehendi potest in ullo loco scripturae.

pass_a.467: To firm that reason of yours you cite the Apostle proving Abraham was justified because he believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. Who would ever have hoped from that to get Adam's first actual sin immediately imputed to all humans—and indeed unto this penalty, hereditary corruption? For that is our question, whose affirmation you had formally to conclude. You must be a subtle and wondrous craftsman of arguments who can forge that imputation from such places.
pass_a.468: But what do you conclude from it? As a man is justified and blessed because he believes in him who justifies the ungodly, and his faith is imputed for righteousness without works because sin is not imputed, so by the rule of contraries one who does not believe is damned and miserable because sin is imputed to him unto condemnation—Placeus grants. And in general every sin he committed—he admits. And in species this sin of Adam that constitutes him a sinner—this Placeus now denies, if by Adam's sin you mean his actual sin and immediate imputation.
pass_a.469: Chamier says that constitutes us sinners causally, not formally—more on that in its place. Those were the only OT finds you thought could clinch the charge. Placeus could have stacked great divines behind his answers and mined the same texts for counters; he prefers brevity and will not bury the reader under argument-heaps.
pass_a.470: Texts about God visiting fathers' guilt on sons are skipped here on purpose: they serve better as a shield against Placeus than as a proof of charging Adam's actual deed. Nothing follows from them that would not also follow for Adam's other sins and for other parents; the stop at the fourth generation fights an unlimited charge across all ages; and 'those who hate me' already assumes hatred in the visited—whereas your charge of the first actual assumes no infant vice but, if believed, creates it. More on those places elsewhere.
pass_a.471: Now Placeus may argue thus: If the dogma of imputing Adam's first actual sin to all and each human is true and to be believed, it is surely revealed somewhere in the Old Testament. But it is revealed nowhere in the Old Testament. Therefore it is not true and to be believed. The minor is clear from this dispute. He proves the major because the law is fitted to detect and lay open sin: through the law is knowledge of sin. It does not do that office as it ought if it does not lay open that sin common to all humans, cause of all others, on which all humans' condemnation hangs. And on your view—who will have that kind of sin be Adam's first actual imputed to all—it does not lay it open unless this imputation can be gathered from the law or Old Testament.
pass_a.472: Further: if that actual deed is charged to all near at hand, and people must believe it, the charge leans on some law—and a very old one—by which it must also be known. No such law turns up in the Old Testament, so that charge must be denied. Unbelieving Israelites who died before Christ were judged by Moses' law from God's hand; by that law they could not be damned at once for Adam's actual deed, nor have it charged, unless the law showed that deed was each one's own. Same for everyone else. Every judicial charge of sin and laying on of penalty runs by some law. Your immediate charge of the actual deed and fixing of sticking vice, if real, is judicial—so by some law. Show that law if you can. Scripture nowhere yields it. Tip: Cap. VIII OT ends; Cap. IX opens NT / Rom 5.

467: To firm this reason of yours you cite the Apostle's reasoning proving that Abraham was justified because he believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. Who would ever have hoped that from there it could be effected that Adam's first actual sin is immediately imputed to all humans, and indeed unto this penalty, namely hereditary corruption? For this is our question, whose affirmation was formally to be concluded by you. You must indeed be subtle, and a wondrous craftsman of arguments, who can fashion that imputation from places of this kind.
468: But what do you conclude from there? (for to transfer all your words hither would be laborious, and not necessary.) Just as, then, you say, a man is justified and blessed because he believes in him who justifies the ungodly; and his faith is imputed to him for righteousness without works, because sin is not imputed, it follows by the rule of contraries that a man is damned and miserable who does not believe in God, because sin is imputed to him unto condemnation. I concede. You add, and in general every sin which he committed. I admit. You subjoin, and in species this sin of Adam, which constitutes him a sinner. This I now deny, if, as is fair, by Adam's sin you understand his actual sin, and also immediate imputation.
469: For that (as most learned Chamier has it) constitutes us sinners not formally, but causally; of which matter in its place. These alone you found in the Old Testament by which you thought that imputation could be concluded. I could also have propped my replies with the authority of great Theologians, and from the same places drawn forth other arguments hostile to yours: but I consult brevity, and I do not wish to weary you as reader with too great a flood of arguments.
470: The places in which God is said to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons are not even commemorated here: for you saw that they are more fitted for defending against my arguments than for proving the imputation of Adam's actual sin. For in truth no argument can be made from them which does not proceed equally of Adam's other sins as of the first, and of our other parents' sins as of Adam's: and that limitation to the fourth generation openly resists an unlimited imputation to all generations: and that other limitation in those who hate me presupposes hatred of God in those who are visited: whereas the imputation of the first actual sin presupposes no vice in infants, but, if you are believed, makes it. But of these places elsewhere.
471: Now I may argue thus. If the dogma of the imputation of Adam's first actual sin to all and each human is true and to be believed, it is surely revealed somewhere in the Old Testament. But it is revealed nowhere in the Old Testament. Therefore it is not true and to be believed. The minor is clear from this our dispute. I prove the major, because the law is fitted to detect and lay open sin: through the law is knowledge of sin. But it does not discharge this its office as it ought, if it does not lay open that sin which is common to all humans, which is the cause of all others, whence the condemnation of all humans hangs. But it does not lay it open according to your opinion, who will have a sin of that kind be Adam's first actual sin imputed to all humans, unless this imputation can be gathered from the law, or the Old Testament.
472: Next, if that actual sin is proximately imputed to all, and humans are bound to believe it, that imputation rests on some law, by whose help it must also be known, and that a very ancient one. Since therefore no such law occurs in the Old Testament, it must be confessed that there is no such imputation. Finally unbelieving Israelites who died before Christ's coming were judged according to the law which they received from God by the hand of Moses. But according to the law they could not be damned immediately for Adam's actual sin, nor could it be imputed to them, unless according to the law it could be established that that sin was the sin of each of them. The same must be said of all other humans. For every judicial imputation of sin and infliction of penalty is according to some law. But the immediate imputation of actual sin to all humans and the infliction of inhering vice, if, as you say, it is, is surely judicial. Therefore it is according to some law. Produce that law, then, if you can. None certainly can be found in any place of Scripture.
